scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Champeta began in the 1970s when commercial trading boats brought African music records to the coast of Cartagena, Colombia.
Afro-Colombian communities adapted African rhythms—such as soukous, highlife, and mbguanga—alongside Caribbean zouk and soca to reflect urban coastal life.
Early groups like Son Palenque and Anne Zwin (Anne Swing) popularized the genre, making it a major sound at the Carnaval de Barranquilla in the 1980s.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The term 'champeta' originally referred to a large knife, and 'champetúo' was a derogatory label used by wealthy social classes against low-income Afro-descendant communities in Cartagena.
As pioneer Charles King noted, the dance and music became a vital expression of community identity and resistance against social discrimination.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Urban champeta is danced as a sensual partner dance.
Dancers position themselves in close proximity, crossing and intertwining their legs with their partner's legs.
The fundamental technique requires moving continuously to the sound of the music without lifting their feet off the ground, maintaining continuous floor contact.
Watch for Intertwined leg shuffle.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical setup of urban champeta features electric guitars, electric bass, congas, electric drums, and synthesizers mixed with African rhythms.
Urban champeta specifically distinguishes itself by blending digital samples into foundational champeta rhythmic arrangements.

A dense coastal blend of driving electric bass lines, melodic electric guitar riffs, and conga hand-percussion layered with digital synthesizers, electronic drum samples, and vocal styles borrowing from reggae and dancehall.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include pioneers Charles King and Viviano Torres (founder of Anne Swing); early groups Son Palenque; turn-of-the-millennium urban champeta stars El Sayayín (Jhon Jairo Sayas), El Afinaito (Sergio Liñan), Mr. Black (Edwin Antequera), Álvaro El Bárbaro (Álvaro Zapata), Elio Boom (Francisco Corrales), El Intelectual (Kevin Florez), Twister El Rey, El Jhonky el profeta (Jhon Einster Gutíerrez Cassianis), El Michel, Hernan Hernandez, Leo Fenix, Karly Way, and El Oveja.
While originating in Cartagena on the Atlantic coast of Colombia, urban champeta spread across the Colombian Pacific region and influenced coastal artists including Bomba Estereo and Monsieur Bugalú.

Urban champeta evolved from 1970s Colombian champeta folk traditions, which were shaped by African soukous, highlife, mbguanga, zouk, and soca, subsequently incorporating 2000s electronic synths, samples, reggae, hip hop, and dancehall elements.
